title: The classifier that loves software
scenario: A finance team uses a model to label expense lines as travel, software, office or other. The labels feed a monthly report that a script parses. In production, far too many lines are labelled software, the label 'other' almost never appears, and about one reply in five starts with 'Category:' and breaks the script. You review the examples in the prompt (exhibit).
exhibit:
Label the expense line as travel, software, office, or other.

<examples>
<example>
Input: Annual licence, design tool
Output: software
</example>
<example>
Input: Cloud storage plan, 12 months
Output: software
</example>
<example>
Input: Flight to Berlin, sales visit
Output: travel
</example>
<example>
Input: Code editor subscription
Output: Category: software
</example>
</examples>

Input: {expense_line}
Output:

questions.prompt: Why does the model over-use 'software' and almost never answer 'other'?

options.text: Most examples are software and none show office or other, so the model copies that skew.
options.explanation: Right. The examples are not diverse. The Claude docs say to cover edge cases and vary examples so the model doesn't pick up unintended patterns.

options.text: Models are trained to prefer whichever label is listed first or most often in the instruction.
options.explanation: 'travel' is listed first, yet 'software' dominates. The pattern matches the examples, not the label order.

options.text: The word 'other' is too vague for the model to ever choose it.
options.explanation: A vague label can be harder, but the bigger signal is that no example ever shows 'other' being used.

options.text: The prompt is too short. Longer prompts always classify more evenly.
options.explanation: Length is not the issue. Four skewed examples would stay skewed inside a longer prompt.

questions.prompt: What is the best change to the example set?

options.text: Add 40 more software and travel examples so the model sees more data.
options.explanation: That keeps the skew and adds cost. The Gemini docs also warn that too many examples can cause overfitting.

options.text: Delete all examples and add 'Use all four labels evenly'.
options.explanation: Real expenses are not evenly spread, so 'evenly' is the wrong goal. Removing examples also loses the format signal.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on last year's labelled expenses first.
options.explanation: OpenAI presents few-shot prompting as a way to steer a model without fine-tuning. Fix the examples first; fine-tuning is a bigger, slower step.

options.text: Use 4–5 examples: one per label, a hard 'other' case, one format.
options.explanation: Right. Relevant, diverse and consistent, in the 3–5 range the Claude docs suggest.

questions.prompt: Why do some replies start with 'Category:'?

options.text: The model adds labels when it is unsure of the answer.
options.explanation: The prefix is a format choice, and the exhibit shows where it came from.

options.text: One example's output says 'Category: software', so the examples show two formats.
options.explanation: Right. Gemini's docs say examples must share the same structure and formatting to avoid undesired formats.

options.text: The script reads the output in the wrong text encoding.
options.explanation: The model really writes the prefix. The fourth example taught it to.

options.text: The instruction line is missing the word 'only', so the model feels free to add text.
options.explanation: 'Output only the label' would help a little, but the examples would still contradict it. Fix the example first.

questions.prompt: The team plans to try an OpenAI reasoning model for this task. What does OpenAI's reasoning guide suggest?

options.text: Double the number of examples, since reasoning models need more data.
options.explanation: The guide says the opposite: reasoning models often don't need few-shot examples.

options.text: Remove the label list from the instructions, since the examples already show it.
options.explanation: The guide asks for examples that match the instructions, not examples that replace them.

options.text: Try zero-shot first; if examples return, keep them closely matched to the instructions.
options.explanation: Right. 'Try zero shot first, then few shot if needed', and discrepancies between examples and instructions may produce poor results.

options.text: Move the examples into the user message so the model treats them as real customer inputs.
options.explanation: OpenAI places examples in the developer message. Examples in the user message blur demo and real input.
